title: HE WENT DOWN INTO THE PIT
paragraphs:
HE WENT DOWN INTO THE PIT
The Snow Was Falling. A Lion Was Waiting. And Benaiah Did the Unthinkable.
There are Bible stories you remember because they are famous.
David and Goliath.
Daniel and the lions.
Moses and the Red Sea.
Then there are verses hiding in plain sight that make you stop, read them again, and whisper:
Wait… he did what?
This is one of them.

Buried among the names and exploits of David’s mighty men is a sentence so strange, so violent, so cinematic, and so unexpectedly human that it almost sounds like somebody slipped an action scene into the Old Testament.
But it is there.
Benaiah.
Son of Jehoiada.
A warrior from Kabzeel.
Snow falling.
A pit.
A lion.
And instead of staying safely above it…
he went down.
The King James Version preserves the stark simplicity of the moment:
“And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada… went down also and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow.” — 2 Samuel 23:20
The parallel account in 1 Chronicles 11:22 records the same extraordinary event.
Read those words carefully.
He went down.
The Hebrew behind the phrase is וְהוּא יָרַד — vehu yarad — essentially, “and he went down.”
Not “he accidentally fell.”
Not “he was pushed.”
Not “the lion dragged him in.”
The biblical text tells us that Benaiah went down.

We should also be careful not to make Scripture say more than Scripture actually says. You may have heard this preached as Benaiah “chasing” the lion into the pit or “jumping” after it. Those images are dramatic, but the Hebrew text itself simply tells us that he went down and struck the lion in the pit.
And somehow…
that makes the story even more haunting.
Because Scripture does not tell us what Benaiah was thinking.
It does not tell us why the lion was there.
It does not tell us whether Benaiah was terrified.
It does not describe the fight.
It gives us something far more unforgettable:
a man went down…
and came back out.
Maybe that is why this strange little verse has survived in the imagination of believers for generations.
Because sooner or later, everybody discovers a pit.
Maybe yours does not have snow around it.
Maybe yours does not have claws.
But you know what it feels like to stand at the edge of something you desperately wish God would remove.
The diagnosis you never expected.
The marriage that became painfully cold.
The temptation you promised Jesus you would never return to.
The secret browser history.
The addiction nobody at church knows about.
The child who stopped answering your calls.
The betrayal that changed the way you trust people.
The bills sitting unopened because looking at them makes your chest tighten.
The grief that waits until everybody goes home.
The ministry wound you smile through on Sunday.
The private shame underneath your public worship.
The night you whispered, “God, I don't know how much longer I can do this.”
We want Christianity to mean that lions disappear.
Sometimes they don't.
We want obedience to guarantee warm weather.
Sometimes snow falls.
We want faithfulness to mean there will never be pits.
Sometimes the road God permits us to walk passes directly beside one.
And this is where we must resist turning Benaiah into a motivational poster.
Because the Bible is not ultimately a book about discovering the warrior inside yourself.
It is the story of the God who saves sinners who cannot save themselves.
Benaiah's courage is real.
His exploit is extraordinary.
But Benaiah is not Jesus.
And neither are you.
That matters.
Because if you read this story merely as “be fearless like Benaiah,” eventually life will give you a lion bigger than your courage.
Eventually your strength runs out.
Eventually your hands shake.
Eventually there is something you cannot defeat.
Eventually every human being reaches the enemy no warrior can overcome by determination:
death.
And that is where the Gospel becomes infinitely greater than motivational Christianity.
Jesus did not come merely to teach frightened people how to become braver.
He came to rescue the guilty.
He came for sinners.
He came for rebels.
He came for hypocrites.
He came for people carrying histories they wish they could rewrite.
He came for people who have failed after promising God they would change.
He came for the ashamed.
The sexually broken.
The bitter.
The addicted.
The religious.
The self-righteous.
The exhausted.
The prodigal.
The person reading this right now who knows there is something underneath the surface that almost nobody knows.
Christ did not stand safely above our ruin shouting instructions.
He came down.
That is the greater descent.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He entered our suffering.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with the despised.
He welcomed the broken.
And then He walked toward something infinitely darker than Benaiah's pit.
The cross.
Jesus knew what waited there.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Blood.
Nails.
Judgment.
Death.
And He went willingly.
Not because humanity deserved rescue.
Because grace moved toward people who could never rescue themselves.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin.
Not His sin.
Ours.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant who would be “wounded for our transgressions.”
The apostle Peter would later write that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
Paul would announce the scandalous exchange of the Gospel: the One who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
That is Christianity.
Not:
“Become strong enough and God will accept you.”
But:
Christ was strong where you were helpless.
Christ was righteous where you were guilty.
Christ paid what you could never pay.
Christ entered death…
and death could not keep Him.
The stone was rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly Benaiah walking out of a pit after facing a lion becomes a small earthly echo of something infinitely greater.
Because Jesus entered the grave itself…
and came out victorious.
Yet even here we must keep the biblical picture clear.
Benaiah's lion is not presented in 2 Samuel as a direct prophecy of Satan, nor does Scripture tell us that the pit symbolizes hell or that the snow carries some secret prophetic code.
We do not need to manufacture symbolism to make this passage powerful.
The history is powerful enough.
A real man faced a real danger on a real snowy day.
And within the larger story of Scripture, his courage reminds us that God's servants sometimes encounter terrifying circumstances rather than comfortable ones.
Faith is not pretending the lion isn't dangerous.
Faith is trusting God when danger is real.
Some of you have misunderstood courage because you thought courage meant you stopped feeling afraid.
It doesn't.
Sometimes courage is trembling while obeying.
Sometimes courage is praying while crying.
Sometimes courage is deleting the number.
Sometimes courage is finally confessing what you have hidden.
Sometimes courage is admitting, “I need help.”
Sometimes courage is opening your Bible again after months of spiritual numbness.
Sometimes courage is forgiving someone without pretending what they did was acceptable.
Sometimes courage is walking away from the relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Sometimes courage is returning to church after shame convinced you everybody would judge you.
Sometimes courage sounds less like a battle cry and more like:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And perhaps that is the sentence someone needed today.
You do not have to impress Jesus with your strength.
You need to surrender to His.
Because some lions cannot be conquered by trying harder.
Sin cannot be forgiven by trying harder.
Guilt cannot be erased by trying harder.
Eternal life cannot be earned by trying harder.
You need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe your greatest pit is not what happened to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
That changes the emotional weight of everything, doesn't it?
It is easier to talk about wounds than sins.
Easier to say, “I was hurt,” than:
“I lied.”
“I cheated.”
“I betrayed somebody.”
“I became bitter.”
“I watched things I should never have watched.”
“I abandoned someone who needed me.”
“I let pride destroy something beautiful.”
“I knew what God said and did the opposite.”
“I have been pretending.”
That is where the Gospel becomes scandalously beautiful.
Because Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending your past never happened.
Grace does something far more costly.
Christ meets you in the truth of what happened…
and offers forgiveness purchased with His blood.
Repentance is not pretending.
Repentance is turning.
The Greek New Testament commonly expresses repentance with the word μετάνοια — metanoia — carrying the idea of a changed mind that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Repentance turns toward God.
It stops defending darkness.
It stops negotiating with sin.
It stops calling chains freedom.
It comes into the light.
And the breathtaking promise of the Gospel is that the person who comes to Christ in repentance and faith does not meet a reluctant Savior.
Jesus said:
“him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37
Read that again if shame has been preaching to you.
I will in no wise cast out.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have authority to write the ending when Christ takes hold of your life.
Ask David.
The king whose mighty men included Benaiah was himself a complicated man.
David knew victory.
David also knew catastrophic moral failure.
Adultery.
Deception.
Bloodshed.
Consequences that tore through his household.
Scripture does not sanitize him.
That matters.
The Bible's heroes are not airbrushed.
Their sins are exposed because God's grace does not depend upon pretending human beings are better than they are.
When confronted, David eventually stopped hiding.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a shattered man:
“Have mercy upon me, O God.”
That is where restoration begins.
Not reputation management.
Not excuses.
Mercy.
David's story did not teach that sin has no consequences. It had devastating consequences.
Grace is not permission to sin.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy toward sinners that transforms those who receive it.
And this is why our message remains:
Not because Jesus edits history.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because Christians become perfect overnight.
Jesus rewrites everything because the sinner's identity, standing before God, direction, hope, and eternal future can be transformed through union with Christ.
Condemned becomes forgiven.
Lost becomes found.
Enemy becomes child.
Dead in sin becomes alive in Christ.
Ashamed becomes covered by grace.
Slave becomes free.
And sometimes the person who thought the pit would become his grave discovers that God was not finished with his story.
Benaiah survived that snowy pit.
But his story did not end there.

Scripture later shows him entrusted with significant responsibility. David placed Benaiah over his guard, and in the turbulent transition after David's reign, Benaiah remained aligned with Solomon and eventually became commander of the army.
The man remembered for going down into a pit eventually stood in places of tremendous responsibility.
Do not turn that into a prosperity formula.
The Bible never promises that facing your lion guarantees a promotion.
But it does remind us that one terrible season does not necessarily contain the final sentence of your life.
Your snowy day is not necessarily your last day.
Your pit is not necessarily your grave.
Your failure is not greater than Christ's mercy.
Your temptation is not permission to surrender.
Your wounds do not give darkness ownership of you.
And if you belong to Jesus, your story is moving toward something far greater than earthly success.
Resurrection.
There is coming a day when every believer in Christ will discover that the final lion has lost its teeth.
Death itself will die.
The grave will not keep God's children.
Christ will make all things new.
So maybe today you are standing above something frightening.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you're doing fine.
You smiled this morning.
Answered messages.
Went to work.
Posted something funny.
Said, “I'm okay.”
But your soul knows better.
There is a pit nearby.
And something inside it has been roaring for months.
Listen carefully.
You do not need to prove you are Benaiah.
You need Jesus.
You need the One who already entered the darkness you could never conquer and walked out of the tomb alive.
If there is hidden sin, confess it.
If there is bitterness, surrender it.
If there is someone you need to forgive, begin bringing that wound honestly before Christ.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, stop imagining that becoming “better” will eventually make you worthy.
You cannot clean yourself enough to need no Savior.
Come as a sinner.
Come believing.
Come repentant.
Come empty-handed.
Christ is enough.
Be honest.
There are moments when another believer needs to see that they are not the only person fighting quietly.
Your honesty may become someone else's permission to stop pretending.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you know their secrets.
Because perhaps they need to remember that the pit is not necessarily the end of the story.
Not as a religious performance.
Someone may need the Gospel while everyone else is sending them entertainment.
Someone may need to hear that Jesus still receives sinners.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible.
Someone may need to hear that grace is still available.
Someone may need to hear that Christ is still alive.
Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.

If you want to glorify God through supporting this ministry, do it freely and cheerfully, not under compulsion. Scripture says, “whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should never be done “grudgingly, or of necessity.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Stay close to truth.
Stay hungry for Scripture.
Stay near believers who keep pointing you back to Jesus.
But before you leave, remember the image.
Snow falling.
A dark opening in the earth.
A lion below.
A man going down.
Thousands of years later, we still know his name.
Not because the day was easy.
Because he went down into the place most people would have spent their lives avoiding.
Yet there is a greater name than Benaiah.
A greater descent.
A greater enemy defeated.
A greater victory.
Jesus Christ entered our darkness.
He carried our sin.
He tasted death.
And He walked out of the grave.
So when your past tells you the story is finished…
when shame tells you to hide…
when temptation tells you surrender is inevitable…
when grief tells you morning will never come…
when the pit looks deeper than your faith…
look again at the empty tomb.
Because sometimes the place you were certain would become the grave of your story becomes the place where you discover that Jesus already holds the final sentence.
